title: Near-linear-time short cycle decomposition
formal:
Can short cycle decomposition be computed in near-linear time with only polylogarithmic losses in cycle length and the number of uncovered edges?

Precisely, put \(h(n)=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). Do there exist one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C,a,b,c,q\), with \(q\ge2\), such that the following holds for every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge1\), and \(m=|E|\)?

On the explicit input defined below, using words of \(q h(n)\) bits, every execution of \(A\) halts within
\[
C(n+m)h(n)^a
\]
operations. With probability at least \(2/3\), it outputs simple cycles \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_t\) and an edge set \(R\) satisfying
\[
E=R\;\dot\cup\; E(Q_1)\;\dot\cup\;\cdots\;\dot\cup\; E(Q_t),
\qquad
|R|\le C n h(n)^c,
\qquad
|E(Q_i)|\le C h(n)^b\quad(1\le i\le t)?
\]
Here \(\dot\cup\) denotes disjoint union: no edge may appear in two output pieces. Distinct cycles may share vertices. All constants, logarithmic exponents, and the program are chosen before the input graph.
definitions:
The graph has no loops or parallel edges. Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. The input gives \(n,m\) and an array of \(m\) distinct unordered pairs of different vertex labels, with each pair written in increasing order. These array positions identify the edges; their order is arbitrary. Input entries are binary integers stored in machine words. The algorithm must handle every valid such representation. The additive \(n\) in the time bound includes the cost of processing the vertex set, even when \(m<n\).

A simple cycle is a cyclic list \((v_0,\ldots,v_{\ell-1})\) of \(\ell\ge3\) distinct vertices such that every consecutive pair, including \(\{v_{\ell-1},v_0\}\), is an input edge. Its length is its number \(\ell\) of edges. Each output cycle is written explicitly as this vertex list. The remainder \(R\) is written as a list of input edge indices. The number \(t\) of cycles may be zero. The displayed partition covers every input edge exactly once; the remainder has no additional structural requirement. Every listed cycle must use only edges of the original graph, without adding shortcut edges, contracting vertices, or reusing an edge in multiple cycles.

The word RAM is a sequential random-access machine with one finite program independent of \(n\). Its word length is \(w=q h(n)\) bits. It has a fixed finite number of registers and a word-addressed memory with \(2^w\) cells. Each register and memory cell holds a word-sized unsigned integer; addresses occupy one word, and work memory is initially zero. Reading or writing one word, copying, comparison, conditional branching, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts by fewer than \(w\) positions each cost one operation. Addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, also cost one operation. Shifts discard bits outside the word. Fresh independent unbiased random bits are available at unit cost per bit. Input access, workspace operations, and writing every output word count toward running time. There is no oracle, nonuniform advice, unbounded-precision arithmetic, or free graph preprocessing.

Probability is over the algorithm's independent random bits for a fixed input. The entire output must simultaneously satisfy all the stated conditions with probability at least \(2/3\). On other runs it may report failure or produce an invalid output, but the same worst-case time bound still applies. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case.

In this card, a polylogarithmic factor means at most a fixed power of \(h(n)\), up to a fixed multiplier. The three exponents may differ but cannot grow with \(n\). Near-linear time means the displayed \((n+m)\)-times-polylogarithmic bound, rather than a bound allowing an arbitrary subpolynomial factor.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence statement above or its logical negation. A positive result must specify one uniform algorithm and fixed constants, prove the running-time bound on every random tape, and establish the joint success probability for every valid input graph. A negative result must rule out every choice of program and fixed constants in this model; an explicitly conditional lower bound alone does not establish the unconditional negation.

Existence of the decomposition without the required construction time is insufficient. An almost-linear-time result, or a near-linear algorithm whose cycle length or uncovered-edge bound has an arbitrary \(n^{o(1)}\) loss, qualifies only if its actual bounds meet the fixed logarithmic powers required here. This is a binary algorithm-existence target, not a request to approximate a running-time exponent numerically.
why: A fast decomposition into short, edge-disjoint cycles is a reusable primitive for graph compression that preserves information lost by independent edge sampling. The question asks whether this primitive can match the near-linear running times of other basic graph routines.

context_blocks.text: The task permits a small remainder because a graph can contain edges lying on no cycle. Chu and coauthors established the decomposition framework and its applications to degree-preserving graph sparsification, spectral sketches, and effective-resistance computation. A sparsifier is a smaller graph preserving specified properties of the original graph.

A decomposition with cycle length \(O(\log n)\) and \(O(n)\) uncovered edges is known to exist and can be constructed in \(O(mn)\) time under the usual nontrivial-graph convention. The present question concerns faster construction; it does not ask for a new existence theorem.

Parter and Yogev obtain cycle length \(O(\log^2 n)\) and \(O(n\log n)\) uncovered edges in \(m^{1+o(1)}\) time. Their published near-linear-time alternative allows larger subpolynomial losses in the decomposition parameters. These guarantees do not by themselves give all three fixed-polylogarithmic bounds asked for here.

A February 2024 Toronto theory seminar explicitly identifies the improvement from almost-linear to near-linear time as open. The precise simultaneous bounds and machine model on this card are an editorial specification of that algorithmic question, allowing fixed polylogarithmic losses in the decomposition parameters.

An ITCS 2025 result retains the \(m^{1+o(1)}\) running time with \(O(\log^2 n)\)-length cycles and \(O(n\log n)\) uncovered edges, while proving a near-linear space bound. That improvement concerns memory use rather than the stronger time bound requested here.

progress.text: The framework paper records \(O(\log n)\)-length cycles with \(O(n)\) uncovered edges and a polynomial-time construction, together with faster algorithms having larger parameter losses.
The published ICALP algorithm constructs \(O(\log^2 n)\)-length cycles leaving \(O(n\log n)\) edges in almost-linear time.
The Toronto seminar abstract explicitly lists the near-linear-time improvement as open.
Lemma 17 establishes a near-linear space bound while retaining the almost-linear running time and the earlier polylogarithmic decomposition quality.

notes: Distinguished known existence and almost-linear-time constructions from the requested near-linear-time construction.
Made the allowed polylogarithmic losses in cycle length and remainder explicit with globally fixed exponents.
Specified simple undirected unweighted inputs, edge-disjoint rather than vertex-disjoint cycles, explicit output, and isolated vertices.
Specified uniform word-RAM operations, randomization, joint success probability, and worst-case time on every random tape.
This is the baseline variant with polylogarithmic losses; the stronger O(log n) cycle length and O(n) remainder target is not imposed.

category_assignment.reason: Constructing an edge partition into short graph cycles is a graph algorithm. Algorithms is its single natural broad alternate category.

sentences: The input is a finite undirected unweighted graph given explicitly.
Partition its edges into simple cycles and a small uncovered remainder; cycles may meet at vertices but cannot share an edge.
The target is a uniform near-linear-time algorithm with only fixed polylogarithmic factors in its running time, cycle length, and remainder divided by the vertex count.
Randomized algorithms are allowed with probability at least two thirds that the entire decomposition is valid, while every execution obeys the time bound.
Known almost-linear-time constructions do not automatically meet this stronger running-time requirement.

problem_origin.note: Short cycle decompositions were introduced as an algorithmic framework in 2018. This card selects the near-linear-time, polylogarithmic-cycle endpoint.
